Summary

This paper introduces a new task setting for product attribute mining under limited supervision: expand values for known seed attribute types while also discovering values for previously unseen attribute types, without requiring explicit type descriptions at inference time. To support this setting, the authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories and including titles plus bullet-point descriptions. The proposed method, Amacer, is a pipeline with: (i) syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, (ii) supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, (iii) adaptive expansion of seed clusters plus DBSCAN for residual clustering, and (iv) two additional weak signals for unseen-type discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute/topic-style regularizer. Experiments show gains over OA-Mine and other baselines on the proposed benchmark.

Overall assessment

I think the paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem. The move from closed-world extraction and even zero-shot extraction with named target attributes toward truly open-world discovery under light supervision is meaningful. The dataset effort is valuable, and the paper is generally well motivated. The empirical gains on the proposed benchmark are substantial, and the decomposition between seed-type expansion and new-type discovery is useful.

That said, I have several concerns that prevent me from being fully convinced. The main issues are: (1) the evaluation protocol is somewhat unconventional and hard to interpret, especially the pseudo-F1 built from clustering metrics plus recall; (2) the proposed method is a pipeline with multiple heuristics, and it is not always clear which gains come from better candidate generation versus better representation learning versus clustering choices; (3) the novelty of some components is moderate, with the strongest novelty being in the task formulation and dataset rather than the modeling; and (4) there are some methodological ambiguities and missing analyses around annotation quality, hyperparameter sensitivity, and fairness of baseline adaptation.

Strengths

1. Important problem setting
The paper tackles a realistic scenario for e-commerce: attribute vocabularies evolve, and exhaustive annotation is expensive. The formulation of discovering both new values for known types and values for unknown types under light supervision is compelling.

2. Valuable dataset contribution
WoaM appears to fill a gap between heavily supervised datasets and noisier distant-supervised resources. Including bullet points, not just titles, is especially useful and increases realism. The statistics showing a high proportion of unseen values/types make the benchmark challenging and relevant.

3. Practical candidate generation idea
The syntax/POS-pattern candidate generation is simple, scalable, and apparently effective. It is also computationally cheaper than segmentation-based alternatives and seems to improve exact span quality.

4. Strong empirical improvements on the proposed benchmark
The reported gains over OA-Mine and other baselines are sizable. The ablation between Amacer and Amacer-R suggests the additional weak signals help, especially for new attribute types.

5. Good qualitative discussion
The paper does not oversell the method and includes examples where new attributes are still confused with existing ones. The discussion of topic collapse in latent attributes is also appreciated.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Evaluation metric is difficult to interpret
The biggest concern is the main metric. The paper says it “roughly” treats the average of Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as pseudo precision and then derives a pseudo-F1 with recall. This is not a standard metric, and it is unclear whether it has desirable properties. Since Jaccard/ARI/NMI are clustering agreement measures over matched spans, combining them into a precision surrogate and then mixing with recall may produce behavior that is hard to reason about.

This matters because many conclusions are based on improvements in this pseudo-F1. I would strongly prefer:
- reporting standard extraction precision/recall/F1 more prominently,
- reporting clustering quality separately from extraction coverage,
- and perhaps evaluating type discovery with cluster-level purity/completeness or B3/Fowlkes-Mallows, if appropriate.

Table 5 gives span extraction P/R/F, but it is treated as secondary. In fact, the span exact F1 is low for all methods, which suggests candidate generation/extraction remains a major bottleneck. The paper should make this clearer.

2. Fairness and adaptation of baselines
Several baselines are adapted in ways that may disadvantage them or make comparisons less clean:
- OA-Mine was designed around segmentation; OA-Mine* substitutes your candidate spans. This is useful diagnostically, but not a standard baseline.
- Closed-world tagging baselines are included even though they cannot discover new types by design. Their poor recall is therefore expected.
- It is not fully clear whether all methods use the same encoder, same seed supervision, same candidate pool where applicable, and equally tuned hyperparameters.

The paper would benefit from a clearer statement of what was reimplemented, what code was reused, and how much tuning each baseline received on the dev set.

3. Novelty is somewhat incremental on the modeling side
The overall system combines known ingredients:
- POS-pattern candidate extraction,
- supervised contrastive learning,
- prototype/support-set style expansion,
- DBSCAN,
- self-supervised co-occurrence contrast,
- neural topic-model-inspired latent variables.

The combination is sensible, but the conceptual novelty of each component is limited. The strongest contribution is arguably the task setting and dataset. That is acceptable for an applied/data-centric paper, but the paper currently presents the modeling as more novel than it is.

4. Candidate generation may encode substantial hidden supervision
The POS patterns are derived from product profile attribute values, which are external structured resources. While this is still weak supervision, it is not entirely task-agnostic. Also, the seed set itself is curated from retailer profiles with human consolidation. This is reasonable, but the paper should be more explicit about the total supervision budget and how much domain knowledge is embedded in these resources.

Relatedly, because candidate generation is so influential, I would like more analysis of:
- candidate recall against gold spans,
- candidate precision/noise rates,
- category-wise variation,
- and sensitivity to POS tagging errors.

5. Limited scope of dataset
The dataset covers only four categories, all from Amazon, all in English. This is a good start, but the claims about open-world product attribute mining should be tempered. It is not obvious how well the approach transfers to categories with very different language, to multilingual settings, or to noisier user-generated text. The paper briefly mentions degradation on user-generated content datasets, but this is not central in the presented experiments and remains underexplored.

6. Annotation and test-set quality details are insufficient
The paper says two in-house annotators labeled all reasonable attribute spans and new types, with no overlapping spans and one type per span. But open-world attribute annotation is subjective. I would like to see:
- inter-annotator agreement,
- adjudication procedure,
- guidelines for what counts as a “reasonable attribute,”
- examples of borderline cases,
- and whether new type names were normalized across annotators.

Without this, it is hard to assess the reliability of the benchmark.

7. Methodological ambiguities
A few details are unclear:
- In the supervised contrastive loss, the denominator notation seems unusual; typically positives may also appear in the denominator depending on formulation. Please verify the exact implementation.
- For adaptive expansion, Eq. 2 uses average pairwise cosine within the support set as a threshold. Since cosine distance/similarity terminology is mixed in the text, it is hard to tell whether lower or higher values are better in each equation.
- The latent attribute model uses all unique candidate spans in a batch for the attribute-to-span distribution. This seems batch-dependent and potentially unstable. More discussion is needed.
- The choice of K latent attributes and sensitivity to K are not discussed in the main paper.
- The self-supervised heuristic assumes bullet points within a product discuss different aspects, while spans within a bullet point are semantically related. This is plausible but noisy; some quantitative validation would help.

Questions for the authors

1. How much of the final gain comes from candidate generation alone? Could you report candidate-level recall/precision before clustering for all candidate generation methods?
2. Can you provide standard extraction F1 and clustering metrics separately as primary results, instead of pseudo-F1?
3. What is the inter-annotator agreement on span boundaries and attribute typing, especially for new types?
4. How sensitive is Amacer to:
   - the number of POS patterns,
   - the threshold relaxation parameter delta,
   - DBSCAN parameters,
   - the number of latent attributes K,
   - and the weights lambda_ss and lambda_un?
5. How many human hours were required in total for seed curation and test annotation?
6. How often do discovered “new” clusters correspond to coherent but non-attribute topical phrases rather than valid attributes?
7. Did you try stronger modern embedding baselines, e.g., Sentence-BERT variants or instruction-tuned embedding models, without the latent regularizer?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Rework evaluation presentation
Make extraction quality and clustering quality separate first-class metrics. If pseudo-F1 is retained, justify it more rigorously and show that conclusions are consistent under alternative metrics.

2. Strengthen dataset documentation
Include annotation guidelines, agreement statistics, examples of difficult cases, and a clearer accounting of supervision sources and human effort.

3. Add stronger ablations
In particular:
- candidate generation only,
- supervised contrastive only,
- + adaptive expansion,
- + self-supervised loss only,
- + latent attributes only,
- full model.
This would clarify the contribution of each component.

4. Provide category-wise results
Macro averages can hide substantial variation. Since there are only four categories, per-category tables would be informative.

5. Clarify baseline tuning and fairness
State exactly which baselines were reimplemented, what code was used, and whether all methods share the same encoder and comparable tuning budgets.

6. Discuss limitations more directly
Especially the dependence on POS tagging, English-only scope, and the possibility that latent attributes capture topical concepts rather than attributes.

Minor comments

1. The paper has a noticeable number of grammatical issues and awkward phrasings. It would benefit from careful proofreading.
2. Terminology around cosine similarity vs cosine distance should be made consistent.
3. Some claims in the abstract and introduction are slightly overstated given the limited domain scope.
4. The notation in the losses could be cleaned up for readability and correctness.
5. The significance testing statement should specify exactly what was tested across what units.

Recommendation

Weak Accept / Borderline

Rationale

I lean positive because the problem is important, the dataset appears useful, and the empirical gains on the proposed benchmark are meaningful. I also appreciate the practical orientation and the attempt to move beyond named unseen attributes toward true open-world discovery.

However, my enthusiasm is tempered by the unconventional evaluation, limited methodological novelty beyond the task/dataset, and insufficient clarity on annotation quality and baseline fairness. If this is a venue that values practical datasets and realistic task formulations, I think the paper has merit. If the bar is primarily algorithmic novelty and airtight evaluation, it falls shorter.

Confidence

3/5

I am reasonably confident in my assessment based on the paper, though some concerns could be resolved with clarifications about evaluation, annotation, and baseline tuning.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting for e-commerce, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover values of previously unseen attribute types without explicitly naming them at inference time. To support this setting, the authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and a human-annotated test set. They propose Amacer, a pipeline that generates candidate spans using POS-pattern-based syntax heuristics, learns span representations with supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, and augments this with self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence signals and an unsupervised latent-attribute objective inspired by neural topic models. Final predictions are produced via adaptive expansion of seed attributes plus DBSCAN clustering for remaining spans. Experiments show substantial gains over prior open-world and tagging-based baselines on their dataset, especially in partial-match F1 and new-attribute discovery.
strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and underexplored setting: open-world attribute mining without requiring explicit descriptions of unseen target attributes at inference time.
The dataset contribution appears meaningful: WoaM includes both titles and bullet points, covers multiple categories, and explicitly evaluates unseen attribute types and values.
The proposed method is well motivated for the weak-supervision regime, combining explicit seed supervision with implicit contextual signals for unseen attributes.
The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, efficient, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based alternatives in this setting.
The adaptive expansion step is intuitive and well aligned with the goal of expanding known seed attributes before clustering residual candidates for novel attributes.

The empirical study is fairly extensive, including multiple baselines, ablations, exact and partial span matching, decomposition by seed vs. new types and title vs. bullet points, and qualitative analyses.
The paper is generally clear about limitations and failure modes, especially the difficulty of true new-attribute discovery and topic collapse in latent attributes.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol relies on a nonstandard pseudo-F1 derived from averaging clustering metrics as pseudo-precision and combining that with recall; this metric is heuristic and may be hard to interpret or compare across works.

The method is a multi-stage pipeline with several heuristics and hyperparameters (POS patterns, adaptive thresholds, DBSCAN settings, latent attribute count), making it harder to isolate which components are fundamentally responsible for gains.
Candidate generation remains a major bottleneck, and the reported span extraction precision/recall is relatively low, limiting end-to-end reliability.
The dataset covers only four product categories from Amazon English listings, so claims about general open-world applicability may be somewhat narrow.
The paper acknowledges degraded performance on user-generated content datasets, suggesting limited robustness beyond the curated product-description domain.
New attribute discovery is still only partial: many unseen-type values are either missed or absorbed into existing seed clusters, so the open-world objective is only partially achieved.
Some methodological choices are under-justified, such as the specific bullet-point positive/negative heuristic and the use of average pairwise seed distance as an adaptive threshold.
soundness_issues: The overall methodology is plausible and mostly sound, but several components are heuristic rather than theoretically grounded, especially candidate generation and adaptive expansion thresholds.

The self-supervised assumption that spans within the same bullet point are semantically closer than spans across bullet points of the same product is noisy and may not consistently hold; the paper mitigates this by using a small coefficient, but stronger validation would help.
The latent-attribute objective is reasonable, but topic collapse is observed and not addressed, which may weaken the claimed contribution of unsupervised latent attributes.

The evaluation metric design is a concern: combining Jaccard, ARI, and NMI into a pseudo-precision and then computing pseudo-F1 is ad hoc, and statistical significance on this derived metric may be less meaningful.

Because the seed set is curated using existing product profiles from the same ecosystem, there may be some domain alignment advantages that make the task easier than truly low-resource transfer settings; the paper does not deeply analyze this potential bias.
Despite these concerns, the experiments and ablations do provide credible evidence that the proposed components improve performance on the introduced benchmark.
